findings.title: [P1] Preserve rejection of multiple find roots
findings.body: The new regex captures only the first root and silently consumes additional roots, while the removed code explicitly rejected commands with multiple roots. A command such as `find /tmp /home/user/.ssh -type f -exec rm -rf {} \;` now assigns `/tmp` to `_seg_find_root`. If that first root qualifies for the safety exemption, deletion of files under the second, protected root receives the same exemption. Validate all roots or retain the single-root requirement before trusting the scope of `{}`.

findings.description: The find-root extraction for `find ROOT ... -exec rm ...` was changed from a tokenizer that required EXACTLY ONE non-flag root token (and cleared `_seg_find_root` otherwise, forcing the conservative path) to a regex that captures only the FIRST whitespace-delimited token after `find` and assigns it unconditionally at line 807. Two regressions follow. (a) Multi-root find: `find /tmp/scratch / -exec rm -rf {} \;` now resolves `{}` against `/tmp/scratch` only; the second root `/` is silently dropped, so the rm placeholder is evaluated against a benign path while find actually feeds `/` into `rm -rf`. The removed `_find_root_count -ne 1` guard previously blanked the root for this exact shape. (b) Flags-before-root: `find -L /etc -exec rm -rf {} \;` now captures `-L` as the root (the old loop broke on `-*` and left root empty). The hunk comment claims this 'keeps today's conservative behavior', but the code no longer does: `_seg_find_root` is populated with an option string instead of being empty, so whatever downstream path handles 'unknown root' is bypassed and the resolver operates on `-L`. Because this is a safety hook whose only job is to block destructive rm, any shape that makes `{}` resolve to a harmless path is a direct bypass of the control. I could not read the remainder of the hook to confirm exactly how `_seg_find_root` feeds the protected-path check; the severity assumes an empty root is treated conservatively (as the hunk comment itself asserts).
findings.failure_mode: An agent or user runs `find <harmless-dir> / -exec rm -rf {} +` (or `find -L <protected> -exec rm -rf {} \;`). The hook resolves `{}` to the first token, judges the rm as non-destructive, and allows the command. find then invokes `rm -rf` on every entry under `/` (or the protected root), destroying the host or repository.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the one-root invariant: after the regex match, tokenize `BASH_REMATCH[3]`-through-`-exec` span (or keep the old `[^;&|)]*` capture) and require exactly one non-flag token, blanking `_seg_find_root` otherwise. Alternatively, treat any additional non-flag token before the first `-` predicate, or a leading `-H/-L/-P/-D/-O` option, as 'unknown root' and fall back to the conservative block. Add fixtures for `find A B -exec rm -rf {} \;`, `find / A -exec ...`, and `find -L A -exec ...`.

findings.description: `get_completed_sprints` previously counted only `sprint-1 .. sprint-N` where N comes from sprint.md. It now counts EVERY directory matching `sprint-*` under `grimoires/loa/a2a` that contains a COMPLETED marker, then iterates the find output unquoted (`for dir in ${sprint_dirs}`), subjecting it to word-splitting and pathname expansion. Consequences: (1) stale or foreign directories (`sprint-7` from an earlier cycle, `sprint-1-backup`, `sprint-archive`) inflate the count so `completed_sprints >= total_sprints` is reached before the real sprints are done, flipping the workflow to `complete` and emitting `/deploy-production` as the suggested command; (2) a directory name containing whitespace or glob characters (e.g. `sprint-*`) is split/expanded, producing wrong paths or re-globbing the a2a dir; (3) a project path containing spaces breaks every iteration. The a2a directory is written by LLM-driven agents, so unexpected `sprint-*` names are a realistic input, not a hypothetical. This is a workflow-integrity/decision-gating weakness rather than a direct code-execution issue, hence MEDIUM.
findings.failure_mode: Leftover `sprint-*/COMPLETED` directories from a prior cycle (or an agent creating `sprint-99/COMPLETED`) cause the state detector to report all sprints complete and suggest production deployment while sprints in the current plan are still unreviewed/unaudited.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the bounded loop over `1..total_sprints` (or intersect the found directories with `^sprint-[0-9]+$` and `i <= total`). If find is kept, use `find ... -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' dir` or `mapfile -d ''` and quote `"${dir}"`; never expand `${sprint_dirs}` unquoted. Clamp `completed_sprints` to `total_sprints` before the `>=` comparison.

findings.description: Removal of `_is_billing_class_error` means HTTP 4xx responses caused by account-side conditions (credit balance exhausted, invoice overdue, quota exceeded) are now classified as `InvalidInputError` (terminal, request-side) instead of `ProviderUnavailableError` (chain-walk to fallback provider). This is not an exploitable vulnerability and error messages remain sanitized via `_extract_error_message`, but it is an availability/resilience regression: a billing outage on one provider now terminates the request rather than failing over, and operators debugging will see a misleading 'invalid input' class. Noted for completeness; if the removal was intentional (e.g., to avoid silently routing prompts to a fallback provider on billing failure), document that rationale.
findings.failure_mode: Anthropic returns HTTP 400/402/403 with a billing-class message; the adapter raises InvalidInputError, the retry layer treats it as terminal, and no fallback provider is attempted even though the request itself was valid.
findings.suggested_fix: Either restore the billing-class classification (or move it into a shared helper in `base.py` so all adapters behave identically), or add a changelog/ADR note stating that billing errors are intentionally terminal and update known-failures.md accordingly.
